summary: Collects opinions from the End-to-End Research Group about how the flow label field in IPv6 should be handled, and boils them down to a set of suggestions. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Putting the same colored sticker on every packet of one conversation so routers know they belong together.

questions: how should the ipv6 flow label be used
what is the flow label in ipv6
what is an ipv6 flow label
how should routers handle unknown flow labels
subtitle: Labeling packets to help routers process conversations more efficiently.

tldr.problem: IPv6 routers need a way to recognize which packets belong to the same conversation or flow so they can process them consistently without examining every header field.
tldr.mechanism: The IPv6 header includes a 24-bit Flow Label field that the source sets to the same value for all packets in a flow. Routers can cache flow-processing decisions based on this label.
tldr.outcome: This memo explains how the Flow Label field should be used and the challenges routers face managing it, since the IPv6 spec left several important questions unanswered.

today: RFC 1809 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted. It remains a useful explanation of the thinking behind IPv6's Flow Label field, though many of its open questions have since been addressed by operational experience.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This memo distills discussions from the End-to-End Research Group into guidance on how IPv6 implementations should handle the Flow Label field. The IPv6 specification calls for a 24-bit Flow Label in every packet header, unique when combined with the source address, but left several key questions unanswered.

The memo explains why certain design decisions were made and how routers should handle three critical problems: what to do when they receive packets with unknown Flow Labels, how to remove Flow Label state from the network when it is no longer needed, and which packets should carry non-zero Flow Labels.
sections.eli5: This memo explains the thinking behind IPv6's Flow Label feature and answers the hard questions the original spec did not.

sections.title: What the Flow Label Is
sections.content:
The Flow Label is a pseudo-random 24-bit number assigned by the source host. Zero means no label is in use. For any non-zero label, all datagrams carrying that label must have the same destination address, Hop-by-Hop Options header, Routing Header and source address. A router can therefore look up the Flow Label in a table to decide how to handle the packet without examining the rest of the header, making packet processing faster.

The source must not reuse a Flow Label value until all routers in the network have forgotten about the previous use, to prevent packets from the old flow from being processed as if they belong to the new one.
sections.eli5: A flow label is a number the sender puts on packets so routers can remember how to treat them without looking at the full address.

sections.title: What Routers Do With Unknown Flow Labels
sections.content:
If a router receives a packet with a non-zero Flow Label that it does not recognize, it should forward it as if the label were zero. Treating an unknown Flow Label as an error and dropping the packet would be wrong, because a router might lose its state after a crash, or a source might reuse a label while old state still exists somewhere in the network.

If a flow needs special handling when its state is missing, it can include an option in the packet header to request that treatment. The router will read the option and handle the packet accordingly. This is safer than relying on the router to have state for every Flow Label.
sections.eli5: If a router forgets a sticker, it treats the packet like a normal one. If the packet absolutely needs special handling, it can carry a note asking for it.

sections.title: Managing Flow Label Lifetime
sections.content:
Old Flow Labels can accumulate in the network if sources fail to announce when a flow ends, or if deletion messages are lost. The practical solution is for routers to use a timer: if a Flow Label is not refreshed within some time window, the router discards its state for that label. Each datagram carrying the label acts as a refresh signal, resetting the timer. A source that crashes must wait in a quiet period before reusing any old Flow Label, just as TCP waits before reusing sequence numbers.

The RFC notes this is similar to how TCP initial sequence numbers are managed and suggests the same mechanism would work well here.
sections.eli5: If a sticker stops showing up on packets for a while, the router throws away its notes about it. If a computer crashes, it waits a bit before using old stickers again.

sections.title: Which Packets Should Have Flow Labels
sections.content:
The RFC found the least agreement on this question. Everyone agreed that tiny exchanges (a few packets) should use zero labels, and that real-time flows must always have labels. The debate is over whether TCP connections should get labels. If every TCP connection gets its own label, routers can optimize routes for individual connections. But this could cause routers to maintain so many flow-state entries that their caches thrash.

The memo notes there is no easy compromise: either all TCP gets labels (and routers must handle cache pressure), or none do (and the optimization opportunity is lost). The RFC leaves this for future experience to resolve.
sections.eli5: Nobody agrees on whether ordinary internet conversations should get stickers. Real-time calls definitely should; short chats definitely should not. But long-running transfers are the hard call.

items.title: Uniqueness
items.text: Unique when combined with the source address.

items.title: Consistency
items.text: All packets in a flow must have the same destination address and headers.

items.title: Zero meaning
items.text: Zero means no label is in use.

references.text: Deering, S. and R. Hinden, "Internet Protocol, Version 6 (IPv6) Specification", RFC 2460, December 1998.
